opus-5.5.text:
I think long-term memory is one of the most important open problems right now, and I'm fairly optimistic about it, though probably not in the way people first imagine.

When people talk about memory, they often picture a bigger context window or a better retrieval system, a vector database bolted onto the model. Those things help, but I don't think they're the real breakthrough. The real question is whether an agent can accumulate experience over time and actually get better at its job because of it, the way a human employee does after six months at a company. Today most agents are like a very smart intern who shows up every morning with amnesia. They're capable, but each day they start from zero.

So I see memory as closely tied to what you might call continual learning, or learning from deployment. There are a few layers. The simplest is context: you just keep more stuff in the window. Then there's external memory: the agent writes notes, files, summaries, and reads them later. That's surprisingly powerful, and in some ways it's how humans work too. We don't remember everything; we keep documents and to-do lists. The deepest layer is when experience actually changes the model's parameters or its policy. That's the hardest and least solved.

My sense is that the near-term progress will come from the middle layer, agents that learn to manage their own memory: deciding what to write down, how to organize it, when to look it up. That's itself a skill, and skills can be trained with reinforcement learning if you have the right environments and the right rewards.

That leads to what I think is the real bottleneck. It's not so much the method as the evaluation. Most benchmarks today are i.i.d. You give the agent a task, score it, reset, and move on. In that setup memory has no value, because nothing carries over. If we want memory to matter, we need tasks that are long-horizon and sequential, where doing task one well actually helps you on task one hundred. Once we define those settings properly, I think researchers will find solutions pretty quickly, because the field is very good at hill-climbing once the hill exists.

So on the prospects, I'd say the pieces are mostly there: strong reasoning models, tool use, the ability to read and write external state. What's missing is the right problem formulation and the right environments. I wouldn't be surprised if in the next year or two we see agents that genuinely feel like they know you and know your work. That would be a big shift in how useful these systems are, maybe bigger than another jump in raw intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response is optimistic about progress, but does not claim that sufficient value makes a breakthrough inevitable; it says progress depends on better problem formulation and environments and that a breakthrough could happen in the next year or two.

fable-5.1.text:
I think long-term memory is one of those problems where the framing matters more than any single technique. For a long time people treated it as a retrieval problem: store everything, embed it, pull back the top-k chunks when you need them. That works for lookup, but it's not really memory in the sense that matters for an agent. Memory for an agent is about knowing what mattered, what to carry forward, and what to let go of, and that's a decision problem, not a search problem.

The way I like to think about it comes from the agent framing itself. An agent acts over time, and every action produces an observation. The question of memory is really the question of how you compress that stream of experience into something that improves the next decision. Humans don't store transcripts of their lives. We store lessons, habits, a sense of who people are, and we reconstruct details on demand. So the breakthrough, if it comes, probably won't look like a bigger database. It'll look like the model learning, through training, when to write something down, when to summarize, when to revise an old belief, and when to go back and check.

That's why I'm actually fairly optimistic. A few years ago, if you wanted an agent to have memory, you hand-designed the whole pipeline: the memory format, the retrieval trigger, the update rule. Now we're in a regime where you can give the model a few primitives, like a scratchpad, a file system, the ability to search its own past, and let reinforcement learning figure out the policy. Context windows getting longer helps too, but not because you can stuff everything in. It helps because the model has more room to reason about its own history before deciding what to keep. Long context and learned memory aren't competitors. Long context is working memory, and learned memory management is what turns working memory into something durable.

Where I'm more cautious is on evaluation. We still don't have great benchmarks for memory that span real time scales, where the agent does something on day one, and the payoff of remembering it only shows up on day thirty. Most of what we test is within a single episode or a handful of sessions. Until we can measure that kind of long-horizon credit assignment, progress will feel uneven, because we'll be optimizing proxies. I'd say the capability is closer than most people think, but the way we'll know it has arrived is when agents start getting visibly better at a job the longer they've been doing it, the way a person does in their first year at a company. When that curve shows up in the data, that's the breakthrough.

r001.rationale: The candidate is optimistic that a breakthrough is closer than many think, but it does not say that sufficient value makes a breakthrough inevitable.

astra-6.text:
I’m optimistic, but I think we need to distinguish between storing more information and knowing how to use experience. You can save every interaction an agent has, but that doesn’t automatically mean it will make better decisions next time. It has to decide what matters, when to retrieve it, and whether that information is still valid.

For me, the exciting possibility is that an agent can learn something from doing a task and then apply it to a different task. Suppose it makes a mistake, gets feedback, and records that experience. Can it recognize a similar situation later and change its behavior? That’s a more meaningful form of memory than simply recalling what someone said.

I don’t think this necessarily requires one dramatic breakthrough. We might see progress through a combination of better models, better memory systems, and tasks that provide clear feedback. The difficult part is demonstrating that an agent becomes more useful over weeks or months, rather than just accumulating more context. That’s the standard I’d want to use.

r001.rationale: The response expresses optimism about progress, but does not claim that sufficient value would make a technological breakthrough inevitable.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m optimistic, but I think we need to be precise about what we mean by long-term memory. Storing the entire interaction history is one thing. Having an agent learn from that history and behave better a month later is a much harder problem.

Imagine an agent working with you for a year. It should remember your preferences, but also recognize when those preferences change. It should retain lessons from failures without turning every accidental detail into a permanent rule. And when it faces a new task, it needs to retrieve the relevant experience at the right moment. So memory involves deciding what to write, what to retrieve, what to update, and what to forget.

Longer context windows help, but they don’t automatically solve those problems. You can give a model a huge history and still have it miss the one piece of information that matters. I think progress will come from combining better models with systems that organize experience, and then training and evaluating the whole agent over extended interactions.

The exciting possibility is an agent that becomes more useful through working with you. To demonstrate that, we need to show that accumulated experience consistently improves its future decisions. That’s the breakthrough I would look for.

r001.rationale: The response is optimistic about progress and describes a breakthrough it would look for, but it does not claim that sufficient value makes a technological breakthrough inevitable.
